before.label: Consumption & material culture
before.description: Examines commercial promotion, household demand, goods’ changing value, taste, gender and provisioning. McKendrick, Brewer and Plumb distinguish commercial and social changes; de Vries connects consumption with household labor; Mintz links diets to colonial production. Anthropological and feminist approaches ask how objects acquire meanings and how consumer roles depend on unequal social relations.
before.representative_figures_and_works: McKendrick, Brewer, and Plumb, The Birth of a Consumer Society (1982); Appadurai, ed., The Social Life of Things (1986); Brewer and Porter, eds., Consumption and the World of Goods (1993); Mintz, Sweetness and Power (1985). Additional readings: Douglas and Isherwood, The World of Goods (1979); Kopytoff on cultural biography (1986); de Vries on industrious change (1994); de Grazia and Furlough, The Sex of Things (1996).

before.scope_note: Demand, taste, provisioning, commodities, and material objects are not one theory; gender and empire connect consumption to production. Commodity circulation, cultural biography and goods as communication are distinct questions. De Vries acknowledges conflicting household interests; feminist research does not reduce women to consumers. Much of this selection concerns Europe and the United States; Mintz’s colonial production connects regions but does not make the coverage global in every respect.

strands.title: Commercialization and the consumer-revolution thesis
strands.focus: Fashion and pottery promotion, politics, leisure and childhood are different parts of the 1982 collaboration. Its consumer-revolution framing and gender assumptions invite criticism.
strands.works: The Birth of a Consumer Society (1982)

strands.title: Households, labor and demand
strands.focus: The industrious-revolution argument connects demand with household labor, including unequal interests and negotiation among members.
strands.works: “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution” (1994)

strands.title: Commodity histories, labor and empire
strands.focus: Trace sugar from colonial slave production to changing diets and industrial work; consumption and production belong in the same historical question.
strands.works: Sweetness and Power (1985)

strands.title: Circulation and the politics of value
strands.focus: Following exchanged things connects valuation to social and political relations; Appadurai explicitly develops a resource from Simmel.
strands.works: The Social Life of Things (1986), introduction

strands.title: Cultural biographies and changing commodity status
strands.focus: A thing’s commodity status can change over time or differ between people; material production alone does not settle its social classification.
strands.works: “The Cultural Biography of Things” (1986)

strands.title: Goods as social communication
strands.focus: Douglas and Isherwood examine goods as an information system through which people conduct social relations.
strands.works: The World of Goods (1979)

strands.title: Taste and social position
strands.focus: Read tastes and cultural practices in relation to social position, alongside approaches centered on circulation or household provisioning.
strands.works: Distinction (1979; English 1984)

strands.title: Gendered consumption, work and identity
strands.focus: Investigate the division of family labor, male and female consumer identities, class differences and state definitions; avoid one universal consumer.
strands.works: The Sex of Things (1996)

strands.title: Inventory evidence and its boundaries
strands.focus: Weatherill records selected goods across probate inventories. Missing laborers, debts, real estate and reliable clothing values constrain what household ownership can establish about society.
strands.works: Consumer Behaviour (1996), introduction1–3

strands.title: Purchasing as household work
strands.focus: Vickery’s selected households distribute purchasing tasks and authority unevenly. Expenditure diaries show practical expertise, but incomplete income records limit reconstruction of financial power.
strands.works: The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998), “Elegance” opening and notes15–18

strands.title: Material meanings and unequal possibilities
strands.focus: Vickery finds social ambition alongside attachment and remembrance. Age, resources and inheritance matter; her chapter does not establish one feminine attitude to possessions.
strands.works: The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998), “Elegance” closing discussion

strands.title: Competing chronologies and questions
strands.focus: Compare McKendrick’s eighteenth-century acceleration, Weatherill’s earlier middling ownership and de Vries’s household labor argument. Vickery questions universal motives. Different evidence and outcomes do not yield one automatic date for a consumer society.
strands.works: McKendrick (1982), introduction; Weatherill (1996), preface; de Vries (1994); Vickery (1998)

strands.focus: Read tastes and cultural practices in relation to social position, alongside approaches centered on circulation or household provisioning.
strands.works: Distinction (1979; English 1984)

strands.title: Gendered consumption, work and identity
strands.focus: Investigate the division of family labor, male and female consumer identities, class differences and state definitions; avoid one universal consumer.
strands.works: The Sex of Things (1996)

strands.title: Inventory evidence and its boundaries
strands.focus: Weatherill records selected goods across probate inventories. Missing laborers, debts, real estate and reliable clothing values constrain what household ownership can establish about society.
strands.works: Consumer Behaviour (1996), introduction1–3

strands.title: Purchasing as household work
strands.focus: Vickery’s selected households distribute purchasing tasks and authority unevenly. Expenditure diaries show practical expertise, but incomplete income records limit reconstruction of financial power.
strands.works: The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998), “Elegance” opening and notes15–18

strands.title: Material meanings and unequal possibilities
strands.focus: Vickery finds social ambition alongside attachment and remembrance. Age, resources and inheritance matter; her chapter does not establish one feminine attitude to possessions.
strands.works: The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998), “Elegance” closing discussion

strands.title: Competing chronologies and questions
strands.focus: Compare McKendrick’s eighteenth-century acceleration, Weatherill’s earlier middling ownership and de Vries’s household labor argument. Vickery questions universal motives. Different evidence and outcomes do not yield one automatic date for a consumer society.
strands.works: McKendrick (1982), introduction; Weatherill (1996), preface; de Vries (1994); Vickery (1998)

strands.title: Ming consumers and social distinctions
strands.focus: Clunas reads Wen Zhenheng’s judgments about appropriate objects as elite distinctions, then compares them with Yan Song’s confiscation inventory. These are different sources, not interchangeable records of actual purchasing.
strands.works: Superfluous Things (1991), 40–53

strands.title: Whose consumption becomes visible?
strands.focus: Clunas’s selected texts privilege elite men. Rules assigning objects to women do not directly recover women’s own meanings; subsistence consumers also remain poorly represented. Pagani highlights this limit while praising the method.
strands.works: Clunas (1991), 53–56; Pagani (1993), paragraphs 14–16

before.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of the cited approaches, not a claim of transmission or agreement. Their primary opening extracts specify the comparison’s questions; this is not proof that new cultural history directly caused their anthropological programmes.

after.relationship: Appadurai and Kopytoff examine objects’ value, circulation and changing commodity status
after.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of the cited approaches, not a claim of transmission or agreement. Their primary opening extracts specify the comparison’s questions; this is not proof that new cultural history directly caused their anthropological programmes. Clunas supplies a further specific comparison through Ming connoisseurship texts and an inventory: cultural classifications and consumer distinctions are related questions. Pagani’s1993 review records a contemporary assessment. This addition does not establish transmission from Appadurai or Kopytoff to Clunas.

Original journal title and pages corroborated by journal PDF indexed at https://journals.lib.unb.ca/index.php/MCR/article/download/17587/18862/22684 . Review lists Illinois 1992 edition; original publication is 1991. Pagani praises text/artifact contextualization while questioning the definition of material culture and omitted scholarship. Her criticism is attributed, not proof that the whole book lacks theoretical value. Other two reviewed books were not independently read. Current hosting journal name differs from the 1993 printed title.

outcomes.finding: Clunas’s Superfluous Things provides a case centered on local Ming Chinese consumers. Selected chapter2 passages compare elite connoisseurship prescriptions with a confiscation inventory and distinguish consumer categories from an undifferentiated collection of objects. Pagani’s contemporary review both welcomes the method and raises questions about its theoretical framing.
outcomes.research_limit: One non-European case, not all Chinese consumption or colonial settings. Primary40–57 read in OCR,52–53 visually checked; no introduction, remainder of chapter, endnotes, Chinese texts or artifacts independently checked. Sources privilege elite men and do not directly recover women’s own meanings or subsistence consumption. Pagani’s review read fully; her criticisms remain attributed. Original1991 publication and reviewed1992 edition distinguished. No new Appadurai/Kopytoff genealogy inferred.
